newsitem.title: JAPAN: Weaker yen pushes Honda profits into overdrive.
newsitem.headline: Weaker yen pushes Honda profits into overdrive.

text.p: Honda Motor Co Ltd announced on Tuesday that its profits more than tripled in the last business year as the weaker yen galvanised overseas sales, and predicted another good performance this year.

Japan's third largest automaker said its group net profit for the year which ended on March 31 rose 212.4 percent year-on-year to a record 221.17 billion yen ($1.97 billion). The profit surpassed the previous record of 146.5 billion yen ($1.30 billion) in the year ended February 1986.
Its group sales also rose 24.5 percent to a record level.

Honda is the first of Japan's auto giants to announce its annual earnings for 1996/97 and the pattern is likely to be repeated by the other big names, which enjoyed a similar windfall from the weaker yen.
Honda, whose profits have also benefitted from cost-cutting, said it expected its group net profit to rise a year-on-year 13 percent in 1997/98 to 250 billion yen ($2.23 billion).

"The increase in revenue was led primarily by higher unit sales of automobiles in Japan and major overseas markets. In addition, the depreciation of the yen positively affected revenue," Honda said in a statement.
Honda said its group car sales in 1996/97 totalled 2.18 million units, 15.7 percent higher than the previous year. Its automobile business revenue for the year rose 27.7 percent.
"Favourable sales in major automobile markets, in particular newly introduced models in Japan and North America, were primarily responsible for the increase in sales," Honda said.
Honda said it would further increase car sales in 1997/98, especially in North America and Japan.
The company saw its group car sales growing further to 2.36 million units this business year, up 8.1 percent from a year earlier, Satoshi Aoki, a Honda director, told reporters.
Honda's group business result includes earnings by Honda and its subsidiaries both in Japan and abroad.
Honda's parent current profit in 1996/97 also hit a record 166.62 billion yen ($1.48 billion), 3.5 times larger than the year-ago level. It saw the profit rising 14 percent in 1997/98.
The yen averaged 112.70 yen to the dollar during the last business year, 14.4 percent lower than a year earlier, Honda said.
A weak yen makes Japanese firms' products more competitive in overseas markets and boosts the yen value of sales done in foreign currencies.
Honda used a dollar/yen rate of 115 yen in making earnings estimates for 1997/98, against 110 yen in 1996/97, Honda executive vice president Yoshihide Munekuni said.
A dollar rise by one yen translates into an annual group profit of six billion yen ($53.5 million) for Honda, he added.

Ongoing restructuring efforts also helped push up Honda's profits, trimming costs by 79.50 billion yen ($709 million) in 1996/97, Honda said. It saw some 40 billion yen ($357 million) of cost reductions in the current fiscal year.

"Honda is likely to achieve its profit target for 1997/98, bit it depends on sales at home and abroad," Kankaku Research senior analyst Nobuaki Yanachi said. He said Honda may suffer a larger than expected drop in its domestic car sales in 1997/98.

Honda said on Tuesday that it expected domestic car sales, excluding mini vehicles, to drop 1.8 percent to 610,000 for the year. "We expect a marginal fall because no new models will be launched this year except the Accord which will be launched in the autumn," Honda's Munekuni said.

Ahead of Honda's earnings announcement, however, shares in the carmaker and other Japanese exporters fell on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, discouraged by the recent strengthening of the yen against the dollar.

The dollar dipped below 112 yen in Tokyo trade on Tuesday to its lowest level since December 1996, due to expectations that the interest rate gap between Japan and the United States will shrink, and on worries about a rise in Japan's trade surplus.
Honda shares closed down 120 yen at 3,630. ($1=112 yen)
